heading: Traditional Principles of Rhetoric (Part II opening): Persuasion, Identification (redux), Other Variants, Formal Appeal, Rhetorical Form in the Large, Imagination, Image and Idea

outline.summary: Classical definitions (Cicero, Aristotle, Quintilian, Augustine); persuasion-to-attitude vs. persuasion-to-action; attitude as incipient act; rhetoric grounded in moral-evaluative opinion
Persuasion as identification through shared language, gesture, image, attitude; topoi as catalogue of identification possibilities; formal assent and collaborative expectancy (Longinus)

outline.section: Other Variants of the Rhetorical Motive
outline.summary: Agonistic rhetoric; advantage as master-term subsuming all psychological drives; timely topics; context of situation (Malinowski); rhetoric as proving opposites

Classical taxonomy of figures (polysyndeton, asyndeton, amplification/auxesis, gradatio, epanaphora, homoioteleuton, bathos); formal devices as arising from functional urgency; amplification as most thoroughgoing device

Six-part oration structure; three Aristotelian kinds (deliberative, forensic, epideictic); three Ciceronian officia oratoris (docere, delectare, movere); each office transcends persuasion by becoming an end in itself; Longinus and Augustine as outer limits

Genealogy: Aristotle → Pico → Bacon → Hazlitt; imagination as motor of action (desire depends on perception, Pico); rhetoric applies reason to imagination to move will (Bacon); imagination as immediate spring of action and ground of identification-through-proximity (Hazlitt)

Image built of identifications; infinite/definite question distinction; unearned increment of image vs. ideological argument; images as condensed consubstantiation-nodes; ideology as species of rhetoric; image and idea continuous, not antithetical

concepts.label: Identification
concepts.gloss: The mechanism behind persuasion: speaker persuades by speaking the audience's language — through speech, gesture, image, attitude, topic — identifying their ways with the audience's. Flattery is the paradigm; identification generalizes to all signs of shared substance.

concepts.label: Consubstantiality
concepts.gloss: The substance-theoretic ground of identification: displaying signs of shared substance (opinions, attitudes, values) serves as the fulcrum of rhetorical appeal. At pp.55-56 Burke explicitly links persuasion-as-identification to 'conditions of consubstantiality in general.'

concepts.label: Attitude (incipient act) — 6th term
concepts.gloss: Introduced at pp.50-51 as a leaning or inclination that is not yet overt conduct. Persuasion to attitude is the more general and foundational rhetorical target; it extends rhetorical analysis to poetic structures and formal devices that produce orientations without demanding actions.

concepts.label: Formal Appeal
concepts.gloss: The persuasive power of rhetorical form as such, independent of propositional content. Purely formal structures (antithesis, climax, gradatio) arouse collaborative expectancy in audiences, priming assent to whatever content occupies the formal slots. Form is itself a rhetorical motive.

concepts.label: Collaborative expectancy (formal assent)
concepts.gloss: The state an audience enters when it begins to participate in the completion of a formal pattern, yielding to its symmetry regardless of propositional content. A species of identification with the speaker's movement rather than the speaker's ideology.

concepts.label: Amplification (auxesis)
concepts.gloss: The most thoroughgoing formal device: extension, intensification, and dignification of a subject. In its purest form (systematic exploitation of a theme) amplification names a process continuous with poetic development, making even a popular lyric 'rhetorical.'

concepts.label: Epideictic (demonstrative) rhetoric
concepts.gloss: Aristotle's third kind: rhetoric of praise/blame aimed at the present, at delight in eloquence for its own sake. Burke identifies it as the hinge between rhetoric and poetic, and as the site where the formal/esthetic motive achieves autonomy from ulterior purpose.

concepts.label: Three officia oratoris (Cicero)
concepts.gloss: Cicero's three duties: to teach (docere, plain style), to please (delectare, tempered style), to move/bend (movere/flectere, grandiloquent style). Each office eventually transcends persuasion by becoming an end in itself — yielding semantics, esthetics, and religious fervency respectively.

concepts.label: Advantage (pleonexia / interest)
concepts.gloss: Burke's proposed master-term for subsuming all classical variants of rhetorical purpose and all scientific psychological terminologies of drives. Can be individual, partisan, or universal; its rhetorical valence is determined by the terministic frame of its deployment.

concepts.label: Opinion (moral order)
concepts.gloss: The kind of opinion rhetoric operates on is not factual (true/false) but moral-evaluative: what the audience finds admirable, shameful, advantageous, or just. It sits 'on the bias' across the epistemic true/false axis. The topoi are a catalogue of available moral-evaluative opinions — i.e., available identification-points.

concepts.label: Imagination (rhetorical function)
concepts.gloss: Genealogical treatment from Aristotle (faculty between sensation and intellect) through Bacon (rhetoric applies reason to imagination to move will) to Hazlitt (imagination as immediate spring of action and ground of identification through anticipatory proximity to future states).

concepts.label: Image as identification-node (unearned increment)
concepts.gloss: The image is 'built of identifications' (p.85): it condenses multiple organizing principles simultaneously, so translating an ideological argument into an image yields an 'unearned increment' of associated meaning — consubstantiality not explicitly contracted in the argument.

concepts.label: Timely topic
concepts.gloss: Aristotle's topoi adapted to modern conditions: a commonplace especially persuasive with audiences living under particular circumstances (a cartoon exploiting unemployment in a period of joblessness). Topical shifts alter which images are maximally effective without altering the underlying universal catalogue.

concepts.label: Context of situation (Malinowski)
concepts.gloss: Nonverbal situational factors that participate in a rhetorical act's effectiveness. Burke cites Malinowski's concept as the principle undergirding a 'rhetoric of bureaucracy' — the semiverbal, semi-organizational tactics of institutional life.

concepts.label: Persuasion to attitude vs. persuasion to action
concepts.gloss: Burke's foundational distinction (pp.50-51): attitude is an incipient act, a leaning or inclination; persuasion to attitude is the more general form, enabling rhetorical analysis of lyric poetry and purely formal devices that produce orientations without demanding overt conduct.

concepts.label: Agonistic rhetoric
concepts.gloss: Rhetoric shaped by a strongly competitive purpose: proving opposites, countering jest with earnest, deploying the war of words. Naturally strong in Cicero (law courts, Senate); relates to advantage-seeking and to Aristotle's view of rhetoric as 'the faculty of discovering persuasive means in a given case.'

concepts.label: Image–idea dialectic
concepts.gloss: Image and idea are not antithetical but continuous: images condense multiple organizing principles; ideas abstract from and organize images. Both serve as 'entitlings' or identifications aligning audiences with causes. The tendency to oppose them (in Symbolist/Imagist esthetics) is a historical distortion.

concepts.label: Rhetorical form in the large
concepts.gloss: The six-part structural form of the full oration (exordium → narration → partition → proof → refutation → peroration), described as 'almost as formal as the movements of a symphony.' Creates large-scale appetite and satisfaction through stage-by-stage progression.

positions.claim: Persuasion was always already grounded in identification and consubstantiality: the classical tradition's various definitions of rhetoric (Cicero, Aristotle, Quintilian, Augustine) are all derivable from persuasion as 'Edenic term,' and persuasion in turn involves communication by signs of consubstantiality.

Formal structures arouse collaborative expectancy in audiences independent of propositional content: once the trend of a form is grasped, audiences yield to its symmetry and thereby become predisposed to assent to its content. Form is itself a rhetorical motive, not mere embellishment.

The image, being 'built of identifications,' yields an unearned increment of meaning beyond any explicit ideological argument: translating an idea into an image activates multiple overlapping consubstantiality-claims simultaneously.

Hazlitt's imaginative-proximity account of self-identification shows that identification is a function of imaginative warmth: we identify more readily with what we can imaginatively inhabit — our future selves, our associates, our causes — because imagination 'in a manner identifies' anticipated states with present being.

The three Ciceronian officia each eventually transcend persuasion by becoming ends in themselves: teaching yields semantics/exposition, pleasing yields esthetics, moving yields religious fervency. This shows the instability of persuasion as a bounding concept for rhetoric.

Ideology is but a species of rhetoric: 'ideology' originally meant the study of ideas in themselves, but in modern usage refers to politically directed idea-systems that have inducements to social choices built in. Image and ideology differ in degree, not kind — both serve identification.

calleja_pim_candidates.rationale: Burke's formal-appeal doctrine (form as creation+satisfaction of audience appetite) is the structural homologue of Calleja's plan→execution→feedback loop. The gradatio example — audience projecting pattern-completion by stage two — mirrors the player's anticipatory investment in executing a game plan.

Formal devices that modulate emotional pacing (amplification's swelling accumulation, bathos's sudden let-down, the three-stage climax) map onto game-pacing mechanics that regulate affective intensity through structured sequences of arousal and release.

The attitude-as-incipient-act maps onto the player's perpetual readiness-to-move between committed actions: the player is always in the attitude-state, oriented but not yet fully committed, which is the kinesthetic correlate of collaborative expectancy.

Hazlitt's account of identification through imaginative proximity maps onto player-character identification in story-driven games: players identify with protagonists because they imaginatively inhabit their situations with 'greater warmth of present imagination.'

The image's 'unearned increment' maps onto game environments as condensed consubstantiation-nodes: art direction, sound design, and spatial layout activate affective, kinesthetic, social, and narrative involvements simultaneously, without each being explicitly contracted.

interlocutors: William Hazlitt (Essays on the Principles of Human Action)
Immanuel Kant (Critique of Pure Reason schema)
Bronislaw Malinowski (supplement to Ogden and Richards, The Meaning of Meaning)
Samuel Taylor Coleridge (stress on imagination and unity)
Thomas Wilson (Art of Rhetoric — infinite/definite questions)

tensions.description: Persuasion vs. formal motive: the classical tradition defines rhetoric as persuasion to an ulterior end, but the formal devices (epideictic, amplification, the sublime in Longinus) reveal a motive in form itself that needs no ulterior purpose. Burke holds both without resolving the tension.

Image vs. idea: the esthetic tradition (Symbolism, Imagism) treats image and idea as antithetical (imagination is to poetry as ideology is to rhetoric), but Burke insists they are continuous — both serve identification — and the supposed opposition is a historical distortion.

Persuasion to action vs. persuasion to attitude: rhetoric's classical purpose is induction to action (ad agendum, Augustine), but Burke shows that attitude is the more general and foundational target, and that much rhetoric — including poetic — operates exclusively at the attitudinal level.

Truth and opinion: rhetoric operates on moral-evaluative opinion that sits 'on the bias' across the epistemic true/false axis — not in opposition to truth, but in a different register entirely. Classical accounts (rhetoric as grounded in opinion, as contrasted with science) obscure this distinction.
